cse-2004-cs-1.approach: Structured programming restricts control flow to sequence, selection and iteration blocks with single entry and single exit, so that the flow of control can be read directly from the program text.

steps.title: What the discipline imposes
steps.body: Programs are built only from **sequence**, **if/else** and **loops** (Böhm–Jacopini), each with one entry and one exit, nested properly.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: With properly nested blocks, the static layout of the source mirrors the dynamic execution order: a reader can infer the flow of control **from the program text** alone. Avoiding `goto` is a *means* to this goal, not the goal itself.

answer.value: be able to infer the flow of control from the program text

optionAnalysis.reason: Indentation is cosmetic; a badly structured program can still be well indented.
Compiled code is machine code full of jumps; structured programming is about the source.
Correct — the stated aim is that the control flow is evident from the source text.
Avoiding GOTO is a consequence/technique used to achieve readability, not the goal itself.

pitfalls: Confusing the means (no GOTO) with the goal (control flow readable from the text).
cse-2004-cs-1.verification: Dijkstra's argument: the textual structure should correspond to the process structure — exactly option C.

cse-2004-cs-2.approach: C passes arguments by value; swap works on copies a and b, so the caller's x and y never change.

steps.title: Trace swap(x, y)
steps.body: Copies of x and y are placed in `a` and `b`; the function exchanges the copies and returns. The caller's `x`, `y` are untouched.

steps.title: Check swap(&x, &y)
steps.body: The parameters are `int`, not `int *`; passing addresses only swaps two address values (and is a type mismatch). To work, swap would need `int *a, int *b` and `*a`, `*b`.

answer.value: swap(x, y) cannot be used as the parameters are passed by value

optionAnalysis.reason: Only the local copies get exchanged.
The function body uses a and b as ints, so passing addresses does not swap x and y (and does not even type-check cleanly).
A function need not return a value to have an effect (it could use pointers); the return type is not the problem.
Correct — call by value means changes to a and b are not visible to the caller.

pitfalls: Thinking that passing &x fixes it without changing the parameter types and body.
cse-2004-cs-2.verification: With x=1, y=2, after swap(x, y) we still have x=1, y=2.

cse-2004-cs-3.approach: Stack 1 grows upward from index 1, stack 2 downward from MAXSIZE. All space is used only when the two tops are adjacent.

steps.title: Layout
steps.body: Push on stack 1: `top1++`; push on stack 2: `top2--`. Free cells are exactly indices $top1+1,\dots,top2-1$, i.e. $top2-top1-1$ cells.

steps.title: Full condition
steps.body: No free cell $\iff top2-top1-1=0 \iff top1 = top2-1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Splitting the array in halves wastes space when one stack is small and the other large.
top1 + top2 = MAXSIZE holds e.g. when both stacks are empty-ish in a symmetric way; not a fullness test.
Declares full when either stack reaches a fixed limit — inefficient use of space.
Correct — the stacks have met; no free cell remains.

cse-2004-cs-3.verification: MAXSIZE=4: push 3 on stack 1 (top1=3) and 1 on stack 2 (top2=4): 3 = 4-1, array full.

steps.title: Insert 10, 1, 3, 5
steps.body: 10 is the root; 1 < 10 goes left; 3 goes left of 10 then right of 1; 5 goes right of 3. This forms the chain 10 → 1 → 3 → 5.

steps.title: Insert 15, 12, 16
steps.body: 15 > 10 goes right; 12 is left of 15; 16 is right of 15.

steps.title: Height
steps.body: Longest path: 10 → 1 → 3 → 5 has 3 edges; the right side has only 2. Height $=3$.

optionAnalysis.reason: 2 is the height of the right subtree path 10 → 15 → 12/16 only.

cse-2004-cs-5.approach: Matching parentheses follow last-opened-first-closed order — exactly LIFO, so a stack is the natural structure.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Scan left to right: push on `(`, pop on `)` (fail if empty). Balanced iff the stack is empty at the end.

steps.title: Why LIFO
steps.body: Each `)` must close the most recent unmatched `(` — the top of the stack.

optionAnalysis.reason: A queue gives FIFO, matching the earliest open bracket — wrong order.
Correct — LIFO matches nesting.
A tree can represent the expression but is not the simplest structure for the check.

cse-2004-cs-6.approach: Level order visits nodes depth by depth, which is exactly the order in which breadth-first search dequeues them.

steps.title: BFS from the root
steps.body: Enqueue the root; repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it and enqueue its children. Nodes at depth $d$ all come out before any node at depth $d+1$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: This is level-order traversal.

optionAnalysis.reason: Preorder goes deep into the left subtree before finishing a level.
Inorder is defined for binary trees and is not level-by-level.
DFS explores depth-first, not level-wise.
Correct — BFS with a queue yields level order.

cse-2004-cs-6.verification: For root A with children B, C and grandchild D under B: BFS gives A B C D = level order; preorder gives A B D C.

steps.title: Check each

optionAnalysis.reason: (iii) is an ε-production, which also violates the definition.

cse-2004-cs-9.approach: Each module is compiled separately, so a cross-module reference stays unresolved in the object file until the linker combines the modules.

steps.title: Compile
steps.body: Compiling $M_1$ alone, the compiler sees only a declaration of the $M_2$ function and records it as an **external symbol** in $M_1$'s object file.

steps.title: Link
steps.body: The linker merges the object files, finds the definition in $M_2$ and patches the reference — resolution happens at **link time**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Nothing is resolved while editing source text.
The compiler handles one module at a time and does not see $M_2$'s definition.
Correct — the linker resolves external references between object modules.
The loader relocates addresses; symbol resolution between modules was already done by the linker (static linking assumed).

cse-2004-cs-10.approach: With one register, whichever operand is computed first must be spilled to memory while the other is computed. Evaluate $E_2$ first so that $E_1$ ends in the register, as subtraction needs.

steps.title: Order E1 then E2
steps.body: Compute $E_1$ into R, store R to temp $t$, compute $E_2$ into R, then we need $E_1$ in R: store $E_2$ to $t_2$, load $t$, `SUB t2` — extra moves.

steps.title: Order E2 then E1
steps.body: Compute $E_2$ into R, store to $t$, compute $E_1$ into R, `SUB t` → $R = E_1 - E_2$. Only one store, no reload.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Evaluating $E_2$ first gives the shorter code.

optionAnalysis.reason: E1 first leaves E1 in memory when R holds E2, needing extra load/store to put E1 back in R.
Correct — E1 is computed last and is already in the register for SUB.
Interleaving is not needed and would cost more spills with one register.
Order matters because the operation is not commutative and the first operand must be in the register.

cse-2004-cs-10.verification: Instruction count: E2-first needs code(E2)+code(E1)+2 (ST, SUB); E1-first needs at least one more load/store.

cse-2004-cs-13.approach: Referential integrity says every C value in $r_1$ appears as a D value in $r_2$, i.e. $\Pi_C(r_1) \subseteq \Pi_D(r_2)$. The difference in that direction is always empty.

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Hence $\Pi_C(r_1)-\Pi_D(r_2)=\varnothing$ always. The other expressions can be non-empty, e.g. a D value nobody references.

cse-2004-cs-14.approach: The natural join is on rollno, which is the key of Student. Each Enroll tuple can match at most one Student tuple, so the join size is at most 8; with rollno in Enroll referencing Student, each matches exactly one.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Enroll.rollno refers to existing students (the intended foreign key), so every Enroll tuple finds its student ⇒ at least $8$.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Maximum $=$ minimum $=8$.

120 would require Student tuples to appear without a matching Enroll tuple, which a natural join drops.
960 = 120 × 8 is the Cartesian product size, impossible because rollno is a key of Student.

cse-2004-cs-18.approach: For a cross-coupled NAND latch, any 0 input forces that gate's output to 1. With S = R = 0 both gates have a 0 input.

steps.body: A NAND output is 1 whenever any input is 0.

steps.body: S = 0 feeds the Q gate ⇒ Q = 1; R = 0 feeds the Q' gate ⇒ Q' = 1, regardless of the feedback inputs. So Q = Q' = 1 (the "forbidden" state, since the outputs are no longer complements).

cse-2004-cs-21.approach: A process must have enough frames to hold every page a single instruction can touch, otherwise that instruction can never complete. That number depends on the instruction set.

steps.title: Why there is a minimum
steps.body: If an instruction faults part-way, it is restarted. All pages it references (instruction bytes, operands, indirect pointers) must be resident simultaneously.

steps.title: What fixes it
steps.body: The maximum number of pages one instruction can reference is a property of the **instruction set architecture** (instruction length, operand count, levels of indirection).

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct — the worst-case pages referenced by one instruction set the minimum.

cse-2004-cs-23.approach: "Some boys …" is existential, so use $\exists x\,(\text{boy}(x) \wedge \dots)$. "taller than all the girls" is universal, so use $\forall y\,(\text{girl}(y) \rightarrow \text{taller}(x,y))$.

steps.title: Outer part
steps.body: $\exists$ pairs with $\wedge$: there is an $x$ that is a boy **and** has the property. ($\exists x(\text{boy}(x)\to\dots)$ is trivially true if any non-boy exists.)

steps.title: Inner part
steps.body: $\forall$ pairs with $\to$: for every $y$, **if** $y$ is a girl **then** $x$ is taller than $y$. Using $\wedge$ would claim everything is a girl.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: $$(\exists x)(\text{boy}(x)\wedge(\forall y)(\text{girl}(y)\rightarrow\text{taller}(x,y)))$$

Inner $\forall y(\text{girl}(y)\wedge\dots)$ says every object is a girl.
$\exists x(\text{boy}(x)\to\dots)$ is satisfied by any $x$ that is not a boy.
Correct — $\exists$ with $\wedge$, $\forall$ with $\to$.

cse-2004-cs-23.shortcut: Rule of thumb: ∃ goes with ∧, ∀ goes with →.
